#5633. REPORT: U.S. Exceeds 200 GWh of Energy Storage Capacity Installed to Date

Rapid Growth in Energy Storage Is Helping Stabilize Electricity Prices and Strengthen Grid Reliability; Industry Urges Congress to Pass Permitting Reform to Accelerate Deployment

LAS VEGAS — The U.S. energy storage industry installed 14.3 gigawatt-hours (GWh) of new capacity in Q3, bringing total installations in the first nine months of 2026 to 48.3 GWh, according to the U.S. Energy Storage Market Outlook Q4 2026 (ESMO) released today by the Solar Energy Industries Association (SEIA) and Benchmark Mineral Intelligence.

U.S. energy storage capacity installed has now exceeded 200 GWh to date as grid operators, utilities, and energy buyers turn to storage to lower energy costs and strengthen grid reliability. After voters sent a clear message in the midterm elections that lowering energy costs must be a priority, the U.S. solar and storage industry is urging lawmakers to send the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) to the President’s desk.

Last week, more than 300 solar and storage companies sent a letter to Congressional leadership urging swift passage of BAAJA. The legislation will accelerate energy storage deployment, reduce project costs, and expand access to lower-cost, reliable electricity for households and businesses.

“Voters made it clear that they want lower prices, and the growing deployment of energy storage is helping make that happen. We’re urging Congress to pass BAAJA to build out America’s energy infrastructure and put downward pressure on prices,” said SEIA CEO Tim Pawlenty.

The outlook for energy storage continues to strengthen, with the report increasing its 2030 cumulative U.S. deployment forecast by 3.7% to 708 GWh across grid and BTM. The revised forecast reflects sustained industry momentum, with U.S. installations up 20% year over year through the first nine months of 2026.

Texas led the nation in utility-scale storage deployment through Q3, adding 12.3 GWh of capacity. Arizona and California followed with 7.7 GWh and 6.8 GWh, respectively. Recent SEIA analysis shows that rapid growth in solar and energy storage helped drive down average wholesale electricity prices by 42% in Texas and 51% in California from summer 2021 to summer 2026.

11 states surpassed their previous annual energy storage installation records in Q3, even with three months remaining in 2026: Colorado, Massachusetts, Utah, Michigan, Georgia, Mississippi, Virginia, Iowa, Montana, Alabama, and Illinois.

“States are moving from targets to centralized procurements,” said Pete Tillotson, Senior Analyst at Benchmark Minerals. “Across utility mandates and bulk capacity contracts, energy storage pipelines are growing as a result of both investment appetite and flexibility requirements.”

U.S. storage manufacturing continues to accelerate, ensuring that more of the batteries being deployed to strengthen the grid are made in the United States. In July, a new battery cell manufacturing facility opened in Tennessee. In October, a new cell manufacturing facility opened in Indiana, bringing total cell manufacturing capacity to 92.4 GWh, a 50% increase.

Utility-scale projects accounted for the vast majority of Q3 installations, with 12.2 GWh deployed, followed by 1.3 GWh of commercial and industrial storage, and 746 MWh of residential storage.

#5632. Allina Health, Sutter Health notch Minn. AG's approval for $26B combination

Allina Health, Sutter Health notch Minn. AG's approval for $26B combination" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Sacramento-based Sutter Health and Minneapolis-based Allina Health's plans to combine have earned the blessing of Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison, a key hurdle that paves the path for a Jan. 1, 2027 close.

The nonprofit systems and the attorney general's office announced Monday an oversight agreement replete with service line preservation requirements and $2.15 billion of promised capital investments. Their deal is set to create a 39-hospital cross-regional health system that would be a major player in Minnesota's increasingly concentrated healthcare market.

"My office has extensive authority to review healthcare transactions in Minnesota: we take it very seriously and with every review, we apply the lens of whether it will help you afford your life and live with dignity, safety and respect," Ellison said in the announcement. "At the end of our thorough review of the transaction between Sutter and Allina, I have determined it passes the public-interest test.”

Per the attorney general's office, the $2.5 billion be invested over five years to increase healthcare capacity in the state. That includes $150 million toward rural care, $50 million in workforce development and the scaling of virtual addiction therapy programs across the state.

The systems also agreed to maintain core services at rural locations for five years, to maintain reproductive and gender care for five years (as it complies with state and federal statute) and to continue Medicare participation and charity care. For Allina's workforce, they also agreed to retain all employees in good standing, honor all collective bargaining agreements and not enforce some noncompete agreements.

Ellison's office will enforce the five-year commitments via a 10-year period of oversight, which will include annual compliance reports from Sutter and Allina.

"In the context where the provision of healthcare everywhere is under serious financial strain and Allina is facing its own struggles, I appreciate that Sutter is entering Minnesota with a mindset of growth and an understanding that we cannot simply cut our way out of financial challenges and maintain Minnesota’s high standard of healthcare," Ellison said. "Sutter’s leadership has a history of delivering on growth and innovation and I look forward to their doing the same here."

Since the nonprofits announced their deal back in March, Minnesota and the Midwest have been the stage for substantial health system dealmaking. Sanford Health announced and closed its acquisition of North Memorial Health, while Essentia Health and HealthPartners in September shared new plans to combine and form an integrated 22-hospital organization.

Sutter and Allina, in a joint statement, thanked Ellison's office for the sign-off and said they plan to close their transaction on Jan. 1, 2027.

"From the beginning, our vision has been grounded in a simple yet powerful belief: people across Minnesota and western Wisconsin deserve a sustainable health system that provides access to high-quality, affordable health care when and where they need it," the statement reads. "With our combined capabilities and more than $2 billion in investment, we will expand access to care, improve affordability, enhance care team and patient experiences and accelerate high-impact research and innovation."

Sacramento-based Sutter Health and Minneapolis-based Allina Health's pending combination took a step forward this week with the signing of a definitive agreement, the nonprofit systems announced Thursday.

The agreement locks in the plans shared earlier this year in a letter of intent—namely, that the cross-market deal would bring more than $2 billion of investment to Allina's markets and that the smaller system would become the "Upper Midwest Division of Sutter Health."

Now the organizations are left with securing state and federal regulatory approvals before the deal can close, which they expect to happen before the end of this year.

“This important milestone brings us one step closer to our goal of partnering to enhance care, support our teams and expand clinical capabilities and research as a strong, nonprofit health system,” Lisa Shannon, president and CEO of Allina Health, said in Thursday's announcement. “With our combined expertise, complementary strengths and aligned missions and visions, I am confident we will be well-positioned to meet the evolving needs of our patients and communities now and well into the future.

Should the deal close, the resulting organization would span 39 hospitals as well as more than 400 primary and specialty care sites that collectively see over 5 million patients annually. The organization would also employ 88,000 people, with 18,000 aligned physicians.

Sacramento-based Sutter Health and Minneapolis-based Allina Health unveiled plans to join and form a 39-hospital, $26 billion nonprofit health system.

The pair said Tuesday that they have signed a letter of intent for Allina to join Sutter. Allina would maintain its brand and regional headquarters but operate as the Upper Midwest Division of Sutter. Under that arrangement, Sutter is also committing $2 billion to bolster care access and patient experience investments in Allina’s Minnesota and western Wisconsin markets.

“This includes establishing new ambulatory and specialty care sites to fill care gaps and meet growing community needs, as well as recruiting more physicians and enhancing AI and digital health capabilities,” Sutter Health President and CEO Warner Thomas, who would maintain those titles should the deal close, said in the announcement. “Building on our complementary strengths and combined expertise, we will build a healthcare innovation engine that accelerates how ideas move from development and design into improving the health of patients and communities.”

The systems said they plan to complete due diligence and finalize terms for a definitive agreement “over the coming weeks and months,” targeting a close before the end of 2026 should regulatory reviews run smoothly. A representative for Allina described the structure of the proposed agreement as being similar to a member substitution but noted that the deal's final structure will be outlined in the pending definitive agreement.

Alongside the 39 hospitals, the resulting organization would include more than 400 primary and specialty care sites that collectively see over 5 million patients annually. The combination would also employ 88,000 people, with 18,000 aligned physicians.

Among the benefits of their proposed partnership, the systems led their announcement with the synergistic technical expertise of their organizations and surrounding communities: Sutter’s immersion in Northern California's artificial intelligence and platform development and Allina’s seat in the medtech and engineering hub of Minnesota.

“The proposed combined system will be uniquely positioned to be a national leader in digital and technological advancements that meaningfully improve patients’ and caregivers’ experiences, while continuing to provide the compassionate care their respective communities have relied on for decades,” the announcement reads.

Such efforts, outlined in the announcement, include AI and digital solutions that would reduce administrative burdens for caregivers along with more convenient appointment scheduling for patients via digital consumer tools.

More broadly, the organizations said they expect the combination will help the organizations bolster physician and clinician recruitment, improve patient affordability and grow their capabilities, “particularly in clinical centers of excellence.”

“We are incredibly excited for the opportunity to harness the collective strength of our two mission-driven organizations to make a difference in the lives of our patients, communities and care teams,” said Allina Health President and CEO Lisa Shannon, who would also maintain those titles in regard to the to-be-formed Upper Midwest Division. “As one nationally leading, locally committed nonprofit health system, we will be uniquely positioned to be at the forefront of innovation, building upon the expertise of our physicians, advanced practice providers, nurses and team members to chart a new path for healthcare.”

Twenty-seven-hospital Sutter is the larger of the two organizations, with $19.8 billion reported total revenue and a $509 million operating income in 2025 (excluding impacts of the to-be-approved 2025 Hospital Fee Program). In the past year, it opened 31 additional care sites, added more than 1,100 physicians and reached 3.6 million patients.

Allina reports $6 billion of revenue with a $95.4 million operating loss and has not had a positive operating margin for the past few years. It operates 12 hospitals and more than 100 other sites.

#5631. Third Pillar Constructing Largest Floating Solar Complex in New York

Crown City Solar will be North America’s first floating community solar project. Phases 1 and 2 are under construction, and the three-phase, 22.5 MW DC complex is expected to be fully operational in 2027.

CORTLANDVILLE, N.Y. — Third Pillar Power today announced it is constructing Crown City Solar, North America’s first floating community solar project, at Suit-Kote Corporation’s Polkville Crushed Stone Facility, an active sand and gravel mining operation co-located with an asphalt plant and storage terminal in Cortlandville, N.Y.

Crown City Solar 1 is the first of three 7.5 MW-dc phases and is expected to begin commercial operation in February 2027. Crown City Solar 2 and Crown City Solar 3 are scheduled to begin commercial operation in October 2027, bringing the site to 22.5 MW-dc in total and making Crown City Solar North America’s largest floating solar complex. The complex takes its name from nearby Cortland, known locally as the Crown City because it sits on an elevated plain over 1,000 feet above sea level.

“Every quarry and reservoir in this country already has a job to do. Crown City Solar shows that those sites can take on a second one: powering their neighbors through a Central New York winter, at a community scale, on a working industrial site. The question is no longer whether floating solar works here. It’s how quickly we can bring it to the next site, like Polkville, and the one after that,” said Jaimeet Gulati, CEO of Third Pillar Power.

Third Pillar identified the approximately 120-acre flooded mine pit as an ideal host for the project in early 2024. Thanks to the collaborative efforts of Suit-Kote, the Town of Cortlandville, and Cortland County, the project team brought this first-of-its-kind project to construction less than two years after securing site control and applying for interconnection. Suit-Kote was acquired by Colas USA, the U.S. subsidiary of Colas, in October 2026.

Crown City Solar also represents a series of technical firsts. It is engineered for the conditions of a Central New York winter, including a ground snow load of 69 pounds per square foot, the highest of any floating solar project in the country. Additionally, the project will float its medium-voltage transformers and switchgear on custom-designed barges—another first for a U.S. floating solar project. Floating this equipment further reduces the use of agricultural land, addresses floodplain siting concerns, and improves electrical efficiency. These firsts reflect Third Pillar’s specialization in floating solar, from identifying and engineering projects on working industrial water bodies to securing the permits and interconnection needed to bring them online.

D3Energy is serving as the engineering, procurement, and construction contractor. The floating system uses Alps’ Solar PV modules, Hazelett Marine’s specialized elastic mooring systems, and Profloating’s floats.

“With more than a decade of building floating solar projects across the country, D3Energy is proud to bring that experience to a project of this magnitude. Crown City Solar demonstrates what is possible with floating solar. We’re grateful for our partnership with Third Pillar Power and the trust they’ve placed in D3Energy to help bring North America’s largest floating solar complex to life,” said Stetson Tchividjian, Managing Director of D3Energy.

Crown City Solar 1 is expected to achieve mechanical completion in December 2026.

#5629. Bernie Sanders Unveils His Plan to Push 'Medicare for All' When Democrats Take Power

— His proposal would implement the program over 4 years

Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) is preparing to use his return atop a powerful Senate committee to push for sweeping changes to the nation's healthcare system, setting up an early test of how far Democrats are willing to go in embracing progressive priorities.

Sanders, a Vermont independent who caucuses with Democrats, is currently the ranking member on the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions (HELP) Committee and is expected to become its chairman when Democrats take control of the Senate in January. His agenda, first provided to the Associated Press, lays out the legislative implementation for proposals that he and progressive candidates championed on the campaign trail this cycle.

At the center is Sanders' longstanding push for Medicare for All, a universal healthcare system that would be implemented over 4 years. The first year would lower the Medicare eligibility age from 65 to 55; expand coverage to include dental, vision, and hearing care; and guarantee healthcare to children through age 18.

"This is no longer a utopian vision. This is where the American people are," Sanders said in an interview with the AP.

The proposals offer an early glimpse of how progressives hope to shape the Democratic Party's priorities after an election that delivered the party control of Congress but also exposed competing visions for its future. With the 2028 presidential election already looming, Sanders is seeking to push Democrats toward a populist economic agenda that he argues has gained broader support.

"I think the election, in my opinion, was a crying out for fundamental change in the way the government does business and the absolute need to protect a struggling working class," Sanders said. "I think this is a time to bring about very significant changes in policies so that we can actually improve the lives of working families."

Sanders Keeps Pushing for Medicare for All

Sanders has long championed a single-payer national health insurance program that would replace most private insurance with a federally administered system providing universal coverage.

His proposal for the new Congress lays out a 4-year transition to that system, beginning with expanding Medicare eligibility and benefits. In the second year, the eligibility age would fall to 45, followed by 35 in the third year, before extending coverage to everyone in the fourth year.

"Transforming a system which is 18% of the GDP of America, you don't do that overnight," Sanders said of the transitional period.

But the costs of lowering Medicare eligibility are likely to lead to massive debate between the two major political parties as the national deficit stands at $2 trillion, or 6.2% of gross domestic product. And the Congressional Budget Office estimated in 2022 that lowering the age of Medicare eligibility to 60 would increase federal budget deficits by $155 billion over the 2026–2031 period.

Sanders' prior proposals to pay for the program shift healthcare financing away from private insurance premiums and toward payroll contributions -- including a combination of employer and household premiums, higher taxes on the rich, and new taxes on Wall Street and large firms.

Sanders also argued that Democrats could pass the first stage of the transition through budget reconciliation, a process that allows certain tax and spending legislation to advance through the 100-member Senate with a simple majority rather than the 60 votes typically required to overcome a filibuster. Democrats will have a 56-44 Senate majority when the new Congress begins in January, marking the party's largest advantage in the chamber in 16 years.

Along with pushing for greater access to primary care, Sanders says Democrats will push for lower prescription drug costs.

Sanders has previously balanced his progressive ambitions with the realities of governing. During his first stint chairing the HELP Committee from 2023 to 2025, he worked with Republicans on legislation to lower prescription drug costs and expand access to primary care. He also chaired the Senate Budget Committee from 2021 to 2023, helping advance major Democratic spending priorities.

But now, just weeks after the midterms, Sanders is laying out an ambitious agenda that he argues reflects a shift not in his own positions but in voters' demands for sweeping changes to the healthcare system.

He sees signs of that shift among Democratic leaders. House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York has pledged to get to work "right out of the gate" to restore Affordable Care Act subsidies and reverse Medicaid cuts enacted under Republicans.

Jeffries said Tuesday that Democrats know that simply returning to the status quo "is not acceptable" and they are preparing ways to further expand healthcare access by lowering the Medicare eligibility age; adding access to vision, hearing, and dental coverage; and ensuring all kids are covered.

"Jeffries basically supported the first year of Medicare for All," Sanders said.

But anything that passes Congress the next 2 years will still need to be signed by President Donald Trump to take effect. Sanders rejected the notion that Trump, a Republican, wouldn't sign something like Medicare for All into law.

"Donald Trump may be crazy, but he is not stupid. He's a smart guy, and he's a very good politician," Sanders said.

Sanders is also preparing to use the committee to advance a broader economic agenda that includes raising the federal minimum wage from $7.25 an hour to $20 an hour and promoting the PRO Act, which would strengthen workers' rights to unionize.

The proposed wage increase would nearly triple the federal minimum, which has remained unchanged since 2009, and could face resistance from lawmakers concerned about the impact on small businesses and employment. Sanders proposes to implement it over a 4-year transition period.

Sanders' agenda also calls for sweeping restrictions on artificial intelligence (AI), including a moratorium on new AI data centers, a pause in advanced AI development, and a ban on artificial superintelligence.

#5628. GTA 6 Has Flock-Like Cameras To Track Your Movements

If you thought you were going to escape the nightmare of our growing surveillance state by blowing off some steam in the sprawling world of "Grand Theft Auto 6" this week, I've got some bad news for you. Just like if you actually boosted a car on the streets of Miami, there are cameras and police databases to keep an eye on your every simulated illegal movement. Just having the fastest car on the map isn't going to cut it anymore. To successfully make Vice City their domain, players are going to have to think strategically.

Video leaked in August showed the main character speeding by traffic cameras. The heads-up display showed three connected dots to indicate the car was being targeted by a license plate scanning camera, according to PCGamer. Passing those cameras will alert the cops to your location, and the you'll immediately enter a red zone where the authorities are hunting for you.

If you keep driving along the route where you alerted the cameras, the authorities will keep following you, just like in real life. The best way to escape those searching eyes of the flock-like cameras (and therefore the cops) is to low-key drive out of the red zone, just like in previous iterations of the game. Cops will also respond in more force (aka you'll gain more stars) if they know for sure your character is the perp they're seeking. Changing clothes, cars and weapons after a heist can help you give the cops the slip, says Techradar.

It's fair to say that the Jalopnik crew is wildly excited to tear through Vice City on some vaguely familiar but, for licensing purposes, completely unique high-end sports cars and grow our own individual empires. Whatever keeps us inside and away from the watchful eye of our tech overlords. When you emerge from your self-imposed video game exile, rubbing your eyes in the full light of day, just know you didn't waste a week of your life. You've actually just helped make real world driving safer.

#5627. The Harm From Plastic Is Happening In Plain Sight

It is known. Plastic is a major cause of the climate crisis, yet governments continue to ignore it.

The Environmental Justice Foundation (EJF) has issued a new briefing published to coincide with the UN Climate Change Conference, COP31, in Antalya, Türkiye. The briefing, “Reducing plastic production in a post-1.5°C world: A test of resolve for the international community,” calls on governments to reduce global plastic production.

Plastic already emits more than two billion tons of CO₂e a year, about twice as much as aviation, and under current policies this would more than double as the fossil fuel industry turns to plastic as its hedge against electrification.

“There’s only so much carbon the world can still emit if we want to avoid blasting past the Paris Agreement targets. Plastic’s harm to our climate is happening in plain sight, and governments are choosing to look away. Every new plastics plant locks in decades of emissions the planet simply cannot afford. As leaders gather at COP31, they must recognise plastic as a major cause of carbon pollution that is rapidly heating our world.” — Steve Trent, CEO, Environmental Justice Foundation

Over 90% of plastic emissions come before a plastic product is even used, during extraction, conversion and production. If current policies remain unchanged, global plastic production is projected to almost triple by 2060, and annual emissions from fossil-based plastics to more than double, to 4.3 billion tons of CO2e.

On this trajectory, plastics would emit 67 billion tons of CO2e between 2026 and 2050. That is just over half of the remaining carbon budget for a 50% chance of meeting the 1.5°C target, and 27% of the budget for a very good chance of limiting the overshoot to 1.7°C. None of this is hidden; emissions are quantified, the projections are published and the industry’s expansion plans are public, yet plastic remains on the margins of climate negotiations.

EJF is calling on governments at COP31 to recognize plastic for what it is: a major driver of climate change that must be tackled at its source, by cutting production.

The petrochemical industry’s bet on plastics

As the world electrifies transport and power, the fossil fuel industry is using plastic as its hedge against electrification. With oil demand for transport and energy expected to decline, petrochemical companies are pivoting to plastics to keep oil and gas flowing. The plastics sector could account for 20% of global oil consumption by 2050, up from around 12% today. The top fifteen petrochemical companies received an estimated US$590.8 billion in financing between 2019 and 2025, and the sector was propped up by state subsidies estimated at over $80 billion in 2024 alone, almost half of which came from Saudi Arabia.

A test of resolve for the plastics treaty

A total of 145 countries from every continent have expressed support for provisions to reduce plastic production during the global plastics treaty negotiations. Rwanda and Peru have proposed a global target to cut plastic production by 40% by 2040 against a 2025 baseline. Modelling cited in the briefing shows that a 40% cut in high-ambition countries, joined by China and emerging producers, could reduce global emissions from plastics by as much as 21% compared with business as usual.

But negotiations have reached a deadlock, driven by a small group of oil- and plastic-producing states, including Saudi Arabia, Russia, Iran and China, with the United States recently aligning with their position. At least 234 fossil fuel and chemical industry lobbyists attended the latest round of talks in Geneva — more than the combined delegations of the EU and its 27 Member States.

Final Thoughts about Plastic and our Leaders

The truth about plastics is perverse. Plastics are widely used around the world due to ease of manufacturing, low cost, stable chemical properties, and good water resistance. They have infiltrated every part of the environment and human life cycle. More than 16,000 chemicals are used in manufacturing plastics, and at least 4,200 of these have been identified as hazardous to human health and the environment. Thousands more chemicals used in plastic production have never been tested. Many of these chemicals migrate out of plastic packaging into our foods, drinks, household products, and bodies.

Researchers have come up with many possible solutions to plastic pollution, as well as ways to mitigate microplastics in the environment. But will governments have the wherewithal to stand up to the powerful fossil fuel lobby that is behind plastic propaganda?

Carolyn Fortuna, PhD, is a longtime journalist and researcher for CleanTechnica who frequently writes about climate science, renewable energy, and environmental communication. Since joining the publication in 2016, Fortuna has authored nearly 1,900 articles focusing on ecojustice, clean technology adoption, and the intersection of science and public policy. #5626. Most nonprofit hospitals' tax breaks outpaced their community spending in 2023: Lown Institute

Most nonprofit hospitals' tax breaks outpaced their community spending in 2023: Lown Institute" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Just over half of the country’s nonprofit hospitals have charity care and community benefit investments that fall short of their tax savings, according to the latest of the Lown Institute’s analyses on more than 3,000 hospitals’ tax filings.

In 2023, the most recent year in which Internal Revenue Service Form 990s were available for review, the think tank identified $38.8 billion of industry-wide tax exemptions, or $12.8 million per hospital and 3.8% of total expenses on average. About $37.1 billion was collectively spent by the same hospitals on various community benefits, as reported in the IRS forms matched to other filings such as Medicare cost reports.

While the total exemption handily outpaces the benefits investments by Lown’s measure, the group underscored that these "fair share” deficits or surpluses also vary widely between facilities, and that some of the industry’s biggest names are on the wrong side of the divide.

Here, Mayo Clinic Hospital led the pack with a $366 million deficit, according to Lown’s analysis, followed by Tisch Hospital (-$294 million deficit), Stanford Hospital (-$255 million deficit), New York-Presbyterian Hospital (-$248 million deficit) and Massachusetts General Hospital (-$219 million deficit).

"Some of America's wealthiest hospitals fall hundreds of millions short of giving back what they receive from their communities, leaving those with fewer resources to pick up the slack," Vikas Saini, M.D., president of the Lown Institute, said in a release on the new analysis, released Tuesday.

Among those leading the latter group were North Shore University Hospital ($167 fair share surplus), Rochester General Hospital ($146 million surplus) and Englewood Hospital ($142 million surplus). Lown’s analysis includes a searchable hospital-by-hospital breakdown of the tax exemptions and community investment totals.

When splitting the 52% of deficit hospitals apart from the surplus hospitals, the former group logged about $15.5 billion above their reported community benefits—a deficit Lown said could wipe the medical debt of 12 million Americans. Fair share surplus hospitals outpaced their exemptions by $13.8 billion.

Total tax exemptions were also “very unevenly distributed” among the hospitals, Lown said. The 30 hospitals, or about 1% of all hospitals, with the largest tax exemptions collectively avoided $6.8 billion, or about 18% of total exemptions. The 607 hospitals, or about 20%, accounted for three-quarters of the country’s hospital tax exemptions.

Lown’s measure of nonprofit hospitals’ tax breaks includes exemptions from federal and state corporate income taxes, state and local sales taxes, property taxes, tax-exempt bonds, tax-exempt charitable donations and federal unemployment tax exemptions. Not included are other benefits provided to many nonprofits, like Medicaid disproportionate share payments, 340B discounts or profits from indirect tax arbitrage.

Its tally of community benefit includes spending on patient financial assistance, subsidized care, payments to other nonprofits to improve health or various community health or social determinants of health investments.

Of note, it excludes Medicaid shortfall—the difference between hospitals’ costs and revenues when treating Medicaid patients—and spending on professional education and research. The hospital industry typically points to these billions of dollars of exclusions when discussing their tax breaks, with Medicaid shortfall alone accounting for nearly half of their preferred community benefit spending totals. Lown noted in its methodology that these accounting losses are often offset by other discounts and supplemental benefits and don’t always have a direct impact on community health, among other objections.

Lown said the disparities between hospitals and the outsized benefits being delivered by some are a call to amend, not eliminate, nonprofit status exemptions. The think tank accompanied its analysis with calls to increase reporting transparency and set spending targets for hospitals tied to variables such as size, exemption value, financial health and prior spending.

“Tax exemptions aren't a gift—they're an expectation, and regulators need to make sure all hospitals hold up their end of the bargain," Saini said.

Lown acknowledged the impending financial pressure hospitals will face with upcoming H.R. 1 policy changes and said such changes should be accompanied by “short-term” financial protections.

Still, the group isn’t alone in drawing scrutiny to the tax breaks. Lawmakers and policy advisors have pointed to, and questioned the justification for, nonprofits’ exemptions when questioning health system leaders on collections policies or high prices.

Academics and researchers have also called for greater transparency or other overhauls of how community benefits are reported or calculated. Of note, a research article published earlier this month in Health Affairs reviewing hospital filings between 2013 and 2022 outlined a disconnect between different hospitals’ listed charity care eligibility thresholds and their relative spending, which more closely aligned with community need than their stated policy.

#5625. No Link Between Gout Flares and Cardiovascular Events in CARES Analysis

— Findings offer reassurance for patients receiving treat-to-target urate-lowering therapy

A secondary analysis of the randomized CARES trial, presented at the American College of Rheumatology annual meeting, found no association between gout flares and subsequent cardiovascular events among patients receiving treat-to-target urate-lowering therapy.

In this exclusive MedPage Today video, Chio Yokose, MD, of Massachusetts General Hospital in Boston, discusses how the findings differ from earlier observational research and why they may offer reassurance to clinicians treating patients with gout who have cardiovascular risk factors.

The following is a transcript of her remarks:

People who have gout experience premature mortality compared to those without gout. And this premature mortality persists even after adjusting for traditional cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic risk factors. And one possible explanation for that that has garnered significant attention in recent years is the possibility that the inflammation associated with acute gout flares may be contributing to subsequent cardiovascular events.

This was really highlighted by a prior observational study using some U.K. data that suggested a temporal relationship between acute gout flares and subsequent CV [cardiovascular] events. But whether this pertains to people who are, with gout, who are undergoing urate-lowering therapy as is recommended by the American College of Rheumatology and EULAR [European Alliance of Associations for Rheumatology] in a treat-to-target approach had not yet been examined.

And so we decided to pursue a post-hoc analysis of the CARES trial to look at the association, if present, between gout flares and major adverse cardiovascular events, or MACE, in this population, which was enriched for people with either known cardiovascular disease or risk factors for cardiovascular disease. And everyone as a part of the original trial were randomized to either allopurinol or febuxostat [Uloric] and titrated in a treat-to-target approach.

Basically, we found about 655 cases who experienced MACE in the trial. We matched them on a 1:5 ratio, so just over 3,200 controls without MACE, and found that compared to controls who did not experience MACE, those who did experience MACE in the CARES trial did not have a higher odds of a gout flare in any of the exposure windows we examined.

And furthermore, we conducted multiple subgroup and sensitivity analyses using different gout flare definitions, looking at treated gout flares, focusing on events that occurred within the first year during this period of intense ULT [urate-lowering therapy] initiation and dose escalation. And all across the board, the findings were null. So in this specific population using the CARES study data, we were not able to replicate the findings of the prior U.K. study. And there was no indication that gout flares that occur in the setting of ULT initiations were associated temporally with subsequent cardiovascular events.

The first takeaway, so when the U.K. study came out, it was very interesting. It was a very interesting and cleverly designed study, but it also raised some legitimate clinical questions for those of us who see a lot of patients with gout and prescribe ULT in a treat-to-target approach. Do these associations apply to ULT-induced, what are called paradoxical gout flares or mobilization gout flares? And if so, if these are also linked to MACE, are we actually doing more harm than good?

And so I think our study, using data from a trial that approximated this very clinical scenario in a population that was specifically enriched for people with cardiovascular disease or risk factors, the fact that our findings were negative, I think, is first and foremost reassuring that we can still continue to recommend treat-to-target ULT for the subset of people with gout who qualify and would benefit from it without worrying that we're inducing cardiovascular events by prescribing allopurinol or febuxostat.

And I do think with the discordant results, additional sort of scrutiny about the differences in the study design, the study population, the definitions used for gout flares, are needed. And there's many ways to take that in terms of next steps.

But I think one very relevant question is it's very difficult to disentangle the effect of gout flare medications from the flare inflammation itself. And while colchicine is considered generally protective for the heart, the other two main anti-inflammatory drugs that we use for gout treatment, NSAIDs [nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs] and glucocorticoids themselves have been associated with adverse cardiovascular events, even with short-term use as would often be the case for gout flare treatment.

So trying to tease out the effect of these flare medications versus the flare inflammation on the subsequent cardiovascular risk in people with gout, I think, is important.

#5624. Voyager 1 Achieves Historic Feat, Making It An Entire Light-Day From Earth

It seems like only yesterday (well, July) I was writing about signals from the Voyager 1 probe taking 23 hours to reach Earth. But as it has for decades, and will continue to do for millennia, the probe that first launched in 1977 has made more progress on its journey beyond our solar system and out to the stars. On November 18, at 5:16:07 a.m. EST, a signal from Voyager 1 will take a full 24 hours to reach Earth — because it will be exactly one light-day from our planet. This is just under 16.1 billion miles, the distance that a photon of light traverses in a single day. If you point a flashlight (a really, really bright one) at just the right patch of sky on November 17, its light will reach Voyager 1 right as it's crossing that point. (At least from the Voyager 1's relative frame of reference; from your reference frame, it will take... well, ask Einstein.)

Nothing man-made has ever gone that far, but of course you knew that, since the Voyager 1 has been the farthest man-made object in the universe since 1998. There is nothing in the works that will overtake it, either. On its journey, it took close-up photographs and readings of Jupiter and Saturn, discovering new rings and moons on both worlds. With its mission completed, it was then granted a second one: to study the edge of the heliosphere, the "wall of fire" that marks the boundary of the Sun's magnetic influence. After itself passing through the heliosphere in 2012, Voyager 1 has been studying the outer cosmos, sending information that takes ever longer to reach home.

Though it will forever traverse the void of space at 38,000 mph, Voyager 1 will not live for much longer. Its plutonium power generator is slowly decaying away, now producing just 230 watts – less than half of what it had when it was young and vital. These days, only its magnetometer and plasma wave subsystem are still performing science research. NASA does hope to keep Voyager 1 and its 68 KB of computer memory powered up enough to make it to its 50th birthday next year, though, and there are some celebrations planned.

Eventually, however, Voyager 1 will send no signals at all. Its plutonium generator will run out completely in the next 10 or 15 years, per Science News. Even before that, it's very likely that its reaction wheels (which keep it pointed in the right direction) will fail soon. Once that happens, it will drift into a spin, meaning its communications dish will not stay pointed at Earth. It will not speak to us, and we cannot tell it how to keep doing science.

The object itself will persist, reaching ever farther out towards the stars, our planet's ambassador to anyone who might receive it. Physically attached to it is the famous golden record, which carries audio and images of a greeting from our species as well as a celestial map that points the way to Earth. So even if Voyager 1 speaks no longer, it will have a lot to say if anyone out there ever finds it, however many light-days or light-years away they are.

#5623. From Social Leasing to Social Fleets: A Proposed Law Lends Credibility to the Goal of One Million Affordable Electric Cars

Social leasing could soon change in scale, name, and business model. The bill introduced by MP Christine Arrighi aims to create a public service offering one million “low-cost electric vehicles” (ALM). Scheduled for December 3rd in the National Assembly, its examination is expected to place at the heart of the debate a now crucial question: how to make social leasing sustainable and widespread?

Several presidential candidates have made reaching one million vehicles (or even more) one of the hallmarks of their campaigns¹. While this convergence is excellent news, the battle of figures says nothing about how to achieve this goal.

The current system cannot simply be scaled up twentyfold. Its cost per vehicle, intermittent financing, imperfect social targeting, lack of a guaranteed solution after three years, and the resale risks borne by dealerships are all structural limitations. The 2026 edition also revealed its dependence on Renault and Stellantis, which can at any time restrict volumes to favor more profitable traditional sales.

The proposed law changes its approach. Sponsored by MP Christine Arrighi, it draws inspiration from the proposals of T&E France and Bernard Julien, stemming from their study on the future of social leasing, published in June 2026.

In this new model, the government would directly purchase the vehicles at an average net cost of €15,000. These vehicles would be kept for twelve years in a public fleet and leased successively to one or more households for an average monthly rent of €150 before being resold. The day-to-day management of the fleet would be delegated to groups of public or private operators within the local areas.

The initial investment to build the fleet would be financed by borrowing, with a maximum outstanding amount of €7.8 billion in 2035. Lease payments and resales, supplemented by €350 million in annual public support (equivalent to the current social leasing budget), would cover service costs and repay the debt within eighteen years. By then, the system would be self-financing, and the state would own one million cars worth approximately €10 billion.

“This model is much more beneficial for public finances,” explains Diane Strauss, director of T&E France. “It requires an initial funding effort, but it eventually pays for itself. Instead of subsidizing at a loss, we build up an asset that generates its own revenue. This is what makes the move to a million vehicles financially viable.”

In addition to providing long-term protection for low-income motorists against rising and volatile fuel prices, the proposal represents a genuine industrial planning policy. The announcement of a public order for two million vehicles over twenty years (including fleet renewal) would indeed give the French automotive sector the visibility necessary to invest and prepare for the future.

“This will also allow us to direct our production towards the vehicles that households truly need: affordable, fuel-efficient, repairable electric cars, produced in France and Europe,” concludes Léo Larivière, automotive transition expert at T&E France. “This proposal must now open a substantive discussion among all stakeholders. It is high time to prepare the next steps for one of the rare examples of policies that reconcile climate, social justice, and industrial planning.”

¹ Raphaël Glucksmann and Marine Tondelier aim for one million vehicles. Jean-Luc Mélenchon proposes a public fleet of 1.4 million cars by 2032, and François Ruffin raises the target to three million. Gabriel Attal and Dominique de Villepin also advocate expanding social leasing, without specifying a target.

Transport & Environment’s (T&E) vision is a zero-emission mobility system that is affordable and has minimal impacts on our health, climate and environment. Created over 30 years ago, we have shaped some of Europe’s most important environmental laws.

#5621. GTA 6 Cars Won't Have Infinite Gas, Hope You're Ready To Fill Up Virtually

As the franchise has evolved over the decades, Grand Theft Auto became a series of sweeping crime epics rather than merely an excuse to boost cars. GTA 6 looks to be putting just a little more emphasis on the "auto" part of its name, bringing Rockstar's signature attention to detail and simulation to all the new cars it has. Case in point: in a game full of heists, shootouts, and epic romance, you will now also have to fill up your car when it runs out of gas. Excitement! Adventure! Joking aside, this new twist may actually add just a little more spice to your bank robbing. Because sometimes, things are most interesting when they're going wrong.

Mechanically, this ought to be less of a burden than driving an actual car, even if it's more than the "infinite gas" of GTA games past. While you're navigating all those cool cars around Vice City's streets, you'll have a fuel gauge slowly ticking down; the game will also tell you once you've hit half a tank and again once it's nearly empty. Nearby gas stations are marked on your compass, so they're easy to find and plentiful across definitely-not-Miami. When it's time to gas up (or charge up, since electric cars are very much a part of the experience), just roll up to a station and hit RT/R2. That will trigger a 10-second cutscene. So, yes, fueling up is part of GTA 6, but also, no, you do not have to sit there and manually pump it yourself.

You might wonder why Rockstar bothered adding this in at all. The point of the game is to have fun, right? A world where you can break all the rules, and the rules (including, you know, physics) are pretty loose anyway. In this case, the key seems to be about giving those crimes a little extra oomph. If you hijack a car, the game is modeling how much gas/charge it has at the time. So once you're getting chased by the police, it's now possible that your newly acquired engine is about to sputter out on you. Then you'll have to leap out of it and try to dodge the cops on foot. Okay, now that is a bit interesting!

In terms of how often you'll be filling up, well, that depends on how much of your time in-game you spend driving. Kotaku ran a few tests and found that vehicles took 18 to 29 minutes to go from full to empty; that can vary based on the car and how you're driving. Keep in mind that crossing Vice City in its entirety only takes about 15 minutes, so this represents quite a lot of driving before you need to stop for gas. And remember, there are lots of stations, and it's just a 10-second cutscene before you're on the road again. Not too bad.

Just in case that's still too much burden for you, there's another option. The in-game Scooter Bros app lets you to call in a vehicle that you actually own (you don't have to steal absolutely everything), so you can swap from one ride to the other. And hey: As extra as this part of the simulation might seem, at least it's not so detailed that you'll ever put gas into a diesel engine.

#5620. HLTH 2026: GLP-1 costs remain a challenge. A new CVS study aims to identify the right price

HLTH 2026: GLP-1 costs remain a challenge. A new CVS study aims to identify the right price" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Cost and access to GLP-1s remains a challenge, but the benefits of these drugs aren't in doubt.

A new study from CVS Health aims to quantify at what price a GLP-1 drug has generated enough savings elsewhere through improved clinical outcomes. The healthcare giant used anonymized claims data from Aetna members in fully insured plans and found savings from reduced hospital and medical spending, as well as improved health outcomes.

But those benefits weren't enough to offset the increased pharmaceutical spending at the current price point, the study found.

The study tracked a mix of members who took GLP-1s from 2023 to 2025, so some patients had three years of follow-up care and management.

Amy Compton-Phillips, M.D., chief medical officer at CVS, told Fierce Healthcare that part of the challenge in this equation is that these drugs gained steam as a treatment for obesity at a high price. And while those costs have come down, the reductions haven't yet been enough to offset the expenditures.

Another challenge for employers in particular—where GLP-1 coverage has been most in flux—is turnover, she said. While GLP-1s do drive significant improvements, an employer may not reap the benefit of the reduced cost if an employee moves to a different company before those are realized, even though they paid for the medication initially.

The study sought to identify a price point where those savings would be felt and landed at $350 per month over a three-year period. Achieving that, Compton-Phillips said, would likely lure employers into embracing broader GLP-1 coverage.

"For them, it might be really worthwhile to say, 'Hey, at this price point, I can afford to cover this for my employees, knowing that in the near term the savings will pay for my investment,'" she said.

The study found obesity rates declining after a 2022 peak, as well as a reduction of between 34% and 42% in hospitalizations over three years. Patients also had 14% lower odds of a serious cardiac event.

For patients who remained on the drugs for three years, their total medical spending decreased by $9,400, but associated pharmacy spending increased in tandem by $13,300, the study found.

Clinical improvements also fell off when patients were not able to remain adherent to the medication over several years, highlighting the importance of a wraparound approach that supports broader care management rather than simply prescribing a patient a GLP-1.

Compton-Phillips said CVS' own weight management program brings nutrition, peer coaching and other supports into the fold, in addition to the prescription. This is especially critical, she said, as evidence suggests weight gain is common after a patient stops taking their GLP-1, making behavior change key.

"At the moment, there's not great evidence that if you come off the drugs, you will maintain the weight loss," she said.

The CVS researchers said that the ultimate goal of the study was not to demand that all GLP-1 prescriptions repay their own costs, but to ensure that drug costs align with patient benefits and the broader cost of access. By lowering the net price of these products, more people can access them, the study concludes.

"These drugs make people's lives better, and I want to give them out," Compton-Phillips said. Doing so becomes a challenge, though, "at the price they are today," she said.

#5619. FDA OKs Drug Linked to Longer Survival in Fatal Genetic Disorder

— Adrabetadex-treated patients with Niemann-Pick disease type C lived longer than external controls

The FDA approved adrabetadex (Lembaz) injection on Tuesday for patients with infantile-onset Niemann-Pick disease type C (NPC), a rare and fatal genetic disorder.

Indicated for adults and children weighing at least 15 lb whose neurological symptoms began before age 6 years, adrabetadex targets the cholesterol that accumulates inside brain cells and drives progressive neurological damage.

The approval was supported by survival data from 36 patients across three clinical studies and an expanded access program, where treatment with adrabetadex was associated with a 55% reduction in the risk of death compared with matched external controls.

Median overall survival was 8.5 years among patients treated with adrabetadex compared with 4.9 years in the control group. Longer survival was observed with adrabetadex regardless of whether patients were also taking miglustat, a therapy commonly used off-label for NPC.

"Niemann-Pick disease type C is incredibly devastating, gradually robbing those who have the condition of all of their abilities, leaving them debilitated and cutting short their lives far too soon. Because neurological function that is lost cannot be regained, early diagnosis and prompt treatment are critical," said study investigator Elizabeth Berry-Kravis, MD, PhD, of Rush University Medical Center in Chicago, in a press release from drugmaker Beren Therapeutics.

Adrabetadex "gives children more time to be children, more time with their families, more time to live life," she added.

Affecting roughly one in 150,000 people, NPC is an inherited lysosomal storage disorder that impairs the body's ability to transport and metabolize cholesterol and other lipids within cells. As these fats build up over time, patients experience progressive neurodegeneration, gradually losing motor control, coordination, and the ability to swallow.

Roughly half of the Americans living with NPC -- about 475 children -- have infantile-onset NPC, the most severe and rapidly progressive form of the disease, in which neurological manifestations develop before age 6 years. Those whose symptoms emerge before age 2 years have a mean age at death of about 5.6 years, while those with symptom onset between ages 2 and 5 years have a mean age at death of about 13.4 years.

Two other therapies are approved for NPC -- arimoclomol (Miplyffa) and levacetylleucine (Aqneursa) -- but neither has been associated with a reduced risk of death, and both have age or weight restrictions that limit access for some pediatric patients.

The most common side effects with adrabetadex (reported in 25% or more of patients in a clinical trial) were hearing impairment, ataxia, fatigue, vomiting, back pain, headache, fever, diarrhea, nausea, and cough. The prescribing information warns of ataxia and fatigue, and carries a boxed warning regarding hearing impairment, including permanent hearing loss.

"A comprehensive hearing evaluation should be performed on patients before starting Lembaz and regularly throughout treatment, and dose adjustments may be needed based on the results of these evaluations," the FDA advised.

A trained healthcare provider administers adrabetadex as an intrathecal injection every 2 weeks.

It turns out, 43 of those people will be soldiers in the U.S. Army's 9th Brigade Engineer Battalion at Fort Stewart, Georgia. While they are being offered four days off from their duties to, you know, defend the nation, this isn't just something the Army is handing out for free. It turns out, dozens of people said, "Hooah!"

As Task & Purpose reports, getting to play GTA for a few days wasn't a deciding factor in whether or not to stay in the Army. Most of these soldiers were already considering reenlistment anyway, so they took the deal as an extra bonus. The bigger idea here was less about incentivizing people to stick with the unit — things like a $60,000 re-signing bonus will handle that — and more about showing that the command sees and appreciates the hobbies of its troops. "We understand you; go ahead and play with your virtual cars," that sort of thing. Is that the kind of leadership that will keep you from entering civilian life? For 43 people, apparently the answer is yes.

This offer was only made to 130 people, so about one-third of those eligible took it. That looks like a relatively successful effort, especially for something that only costs the Army four days of leave per participant. Could Rockstar Games be the answer to the Army's recruitment woes?

Look, not everything the mighty United States military tries is going to be flashy, or even something you'd assume even matters all that much. When you stop and think about it, does it actually make sense? It does, in fact. Humana is continuing its push to reform prior authorization with the launch of a national provider gold card program.

Through the program, eligible providers will no longer need to secure a prior authorization approval and can instead use a streamlined process.

Humana estimates that about 50,000 providers will qualify for the program. Eligible providers must be able to demonstrate a proven track record of high-quality care and patient outcomes.

However, lengthy decision times and other barriers can create a painful friction. So for providers that consistently demonstrate that they are aligned with clinical guidelines, the gold cards can remove that guardrail.

"If they're following those guidelines and providing appropriate care, prior auths don't really serve a purpose for them," Granston said.

The insurer conducted a pilot earlier this year with about 400 provider organizations and approximately 8,000 clinicians. Through that process, the team conducted interviews with clinicians and office staff who shared their desire for fewer administrative burdens and a simpler experience.

Those insights shaped the broader launch, Humana said, and the insurer intends to continue to iterate and evolve the gold card program over time, including by adding new service lines. It's not uncommon for a program to roll out that aims to support providers, but their voice is less often at the table in shaping what the experience looks like to ensure that their pain points are being addressed.

Granston said that the team is examining more time-sensitive services that could fit within the program, for example.

"For our top-performing providers, we would like to essentially get out of the way and let them continue to care for our members," she said.

The gold card program builds on Humana's existing work to reform prior authorization, including a streamlined approval process for electronic submissions that took effect in January of this year. Under this initiative, Humana responds within one business day in 95% of electronic prior authorization cases.

The insurer also announced earlier this month that it would join forces with athenahealth to accelerate the use of electronic prior authorization. Through the partnership, more of the process is embedded directly in the provider's workflow, streamlining the experience for them at the point of care.

Granston said that the goal is to make it easier to surface the data necessary to make an approval and enable that to occur in real time. This also means that fewer people have to be dedicated to the work of submissions and approval.

"When the information exists, you don't really need all these people to be touching it," she said.

#5614. RFK Jr.'s 'Lavish' Gifts; Next Fauci Named; Staff Cuts Tied to Outbreak?

— A weekly roundup of how public health policy is shaping practice

Two Democratic senators are investigating "lavish" gifts, such as flights to Fiji and Greece, given to HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. by a former employee.

Sen. Rand Paul, MD, (R-Ky.) said he is throwing his hat in the ring to become the ranking Republican on the senate's key healthcare committee. (The Hill)

The FDA mothballed a fast-track drug review program instituted under former FDA commissioner Marty Makary, MD, MPH. (Reuters via AOL)

The Trump administration appointed Natalie Dodson, a Project 2025 contributor who has criticized mifepristone, to counselor in the Immediate Office of the Secretary at HHS. (Mother Jones)

John Powers III, MD, will become the next director of the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases, a role that Anthony Fauci, MD, served in for almost four decades.

Meanwhile, Rear Adm. Brian Monahan, MD, the attending physician for Congress, resigned in the wake of investigations into allegations of lax oversight of controlled substances. (Wall Street Journal)

NIH said it will relocate its remaining chimpanzees at one Texas facility to a federal sanctuary in Louisiana.

House Democrats are investigating the "woefully inadequate" response to ongoing measles outbreaks in the U.S. by CDC director Erica Schwartz, MD, MPH, JD. (Inside Medicine)

Democratic senators are asking the HHS Inspector General to look into whether personnel changes at FDA and CDC worsened the response to this summer's Cyclospora outbreak.

And two House Democratic leaders asked the Trump administration for more information about recent actions to disenroll 750,000 people from their Affordable Care Act health insurance plans.

The American Medical Association has asked the Trump administration to abandon its plan to make certain peptides more readily available.

A group of physician organizations asked House and Senate leaders to delay the Medicare payment cut for modifier -25 and extend this year's 2.5% pay increase for another year.

The doctors and scientists elected in this month's midterms are hoping to bring back trust in science, but it won't be easy. (STAT)

#5613. GTA 6 Development Is Hush Hush, But We May Know Where One Car Recording Came From

Rockstar Games may not have created or used any licensed vehicles in Grand Theft Auto 6, but it's possible it's using recordings from real-life cars to make the gameplay sound realistic. The sounds of the older Crown Victoria police cars chasing you in one of your many heists may have been inspired by a young U.K. owner's police car.

About three years ago, Reddit user u/madasafish2010, whom the BBC says is Lukas Holmes, posted in r/GTA6 about his 2009 Ford Crown Victoria Police Interceptor being used for "extensive audio recording" by an unknown entity in 2021. He said he was told that the work was for a Scotland-based company's high-profile video game. His car was invited to the Millbrook Proving Ground in Bedfordshire, England, where Holmes said it was put through its paces by Niki Faulkner, a stunt driver known for his work in "Gran Turismo," "Rush," and "Mission: Impossible — Fallout." In a video about the car, he added that it was covered in microphones and used for several hours that day.

Holmes wrote that he was never told Rockstar had anything to do with the work — he just started putting the pieces together. "It was some firm that was contracted to do the work for game developers, which kinda adds up when you see Rockstar have hired other smaller companies to do their dirty work before." He added, "Niki Faulkner working on a 'high-profile video game project' only led me to one conclusion out of common sense: Rockstar North [is] based in Edinburgh, conveniently the same small country me and my car are both in ... It'd work out cheaper for them to work with local cars than to go abroad and do it."

Owning an old Crown Vic police car was a childhood dream, Holmes told the BBC. He purchased it from the Warminster Township Police Department in Pennsylvania, then imported it to England. He raised money to fund repairs and upkeep via his company Rent-A-Vic, which rented the car to media. It took six weeks of work to bring it back to its former glory, and hours of personal time to recreate the accurate department graphics.

Holmes noted that his car's old-school 4.6-liter V8 has a distinct sound, as do many features like the doors closing, the warning chimes, and the 4R75E transmission. Those sounds, he predicted, would likely be used for the game's police cruiser or taxi.

His dream may have become a reality. In the "Grand Theft Auto VI: An Extended Look" trailer, at 18:24, Lucia (one of the game's two playable protagonists) is speeding in a Dodge Charger look-alike. While speeding, an excited influencer is lying in the open trunk, recording the adventure. On her tail, just barely in frame, is a police car with the Vice Beach Police Department. You have to be quick to catch it, as only the front half of the car appears behind the chat function. Some of the siren audio sounds similar to Holmes' car, as shared in his video.

While the vehicle in this portion of the extended trailer more closely resembled a Dodge Charger Pursuit, other sections of the trailer, like 18:09, show police cars resembling Ford's Crown Vic. In the GTA universe, the Vapid Stainier model primarily bases its design on the Crown Vic. Just note that if you get behind the wheel of a Stainier for a prolonged joyride, you'll have to fuel up virtually after driving at what we assume will be the proper speed limit.

#5612. Fierce Healthcare Fundraising Tracker '26: Aevius launches with $22M for clinical insights; Abby Care secures $82M for family-led care

Fierce Healthcare Fundraising Tracker '26: Aevius launches with $22M for clinical insights; Abby Care secures $82M for family-led care" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

At Fierce Healthcare, we keep track of all the venture capital being funneled into the health tech and digital health industries.

Our fundraising tracker provides updated coverage of noteworthy digital health and health tech funding rounds, though we'll still profile exciting new companies and larger rounds that catch our eye in depth.

Do you have fundraising news to share? Email Heather Landi at [email protected].

Oct. 17—AeviusClinical intelligence AI modelsSeries: N/AAmount: $22 millionInvestors: Led by Insight Partners

Aevius is a newly launched Mass General Brigham spinout founded by veterans of AstreaZeneca-acquired Modella AI. The company builds models that intake different forms of medical data to paint a multimodal picture of a patient's current state and trajectory. That information can then be used by healthcare, payer and life sciences organizations for potential application in care delivery, operational decision-making and clinical research.

“Our mission is to make medicine computable,” Rowland Pettit, M.D., Ph.D., co-founder and CEO of Aevius, said. “As a physician-scientist, I’ve worked across many types of clinical data, and there is far more knowledge in those records than we’re able to use today. We’re bringing general medical intelligence to that data, so organizations can build on a deeper understanding for their patients.”

The company said it plans to use the $22 million launch money to support continued model and product development. It also plans to expand its engineering, clinical and commercial teams, as well as to focus on commercial deployment.

Oct. 15—Abby CareFamily caregiver trainingSeries: CAmount: $82 millionInvestors: Led by Transformation Capital, along with CVS Health Ventures, Frist Cressey Ventures and Pivotal, with participation from existing investors Khosla Ventures, Thrive Capital and Sequoia Capital

Abby Care is an AI-native home care startup that equips family caregivers with professional training, certification and ongoing support from dedicated RN care managers.  The company works with health plans to arrange care at home for families that need it. Abby Care's platform also gives care teams real-time visibility into care delivered in the home, helping ensure families receive the support they need while enabling health plans to verify that care is being provided. Fortune reported the series C round.

The U.S. faces a major healthcare workforce shortage along with a rapidly aging population, and waitlists of vulnerable children needing care, noted Havi Nguyen, founder of Abby Care in a LinkedIn post."Family caregivers already know their loved ones best and are in the home. They’re the first to notice when something isn’t right. At Abby, we equip family caregivers with training, AI, and support from our clinicians to deliver quality care. Our platform enables real-time capture of care data in the home. Health plans and states deserve visibility and confidence that care is delivered as intended. Better care and program integrity go together," Nguyen wrote.

Abby Care functions as a Medicaid provider to pay caregivers within Colorado, Florida, Georgia, Indiana, Massachusetts, New Jersey, Pennsylvania and Tennessee.

So far, Abby Care has helped families deliver millions of hours of care across many states, the company's members had 40%+ fewer reported hospitalizations in year one, she wrote.

Today, the company serves thousands of families across eight states, with additional markets expected to launch soon, executives said.

The funding will enable the company to bring its model to more families, deepen its work with health plans and continue building technology and clinical infrastructure, the company said in a blog post.

Oct. 14—AllswellBehavioral health for LGBTQ+Series: Seed Amount: $7 millionInvestors: Rethink Impact, Magnify Ventures, Ulu Ventures and Hopelab Ventures, Techstars and Amboy Street Ventures

Allswell offers one-on-one virtual therapy, group programs and trauma-informed care to LGBTQ+ patients. It is in-network with commercial and Medicaid payers. The startup, launched in 2025, plans to use the capital to expand beyond its DMV-area footprint, build out its clinical training program for therapists and launch psychiatric medication management next year.

"Nobody realizes how big this market is. Only 5% of Gen X identifies as LGBTQ+, compared with 25% of Gen Z. That's a massive generational and cultural shift, and we want to do for LGBTQ+ health what Midi did for menopause," Heidi Patel, managing partner at Rethink Impact, said in a press release.

Allswell's therapeutic models were built for patients navigating depression and anxiety, identity-specific trauma, family dynamics and social transition. It is also developing its own curriculum on PTSD and trauma care.

The startup, though new, is already seeing positive outcomes. The company often keeps patients for over a year, rare for behavioral health. In its most recent cohorts, 77% showed improvements in anxiety and 71% showed improvements in depression after 60 days of treatment.

"Our patients aren't used to being served with care and respect, or to having something built for them. ... This is a sleeping-giant category, and it has been underestimated at every step. Our ambition is to continue developing new, thoughtful clinical programs specifically for the LGBTQ+ community, regardless of the political climate," Dawn Androphy, co-founder and CEO of Allswell, said in an announcement.

Oct. 14—ReadilyArtificial intelligence compliance platformSeries: AAmount: $11 millionInvestors: Define Ventures led the funding round, with participation from Y Combinator and the California Health Care Foundation Innovation Fund.

Readily’s platform connects regulatory requirements with policies, assigned actions and supporting evidence to reduce manual research and review processes. When the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) releases new rules, CEO and co-founder Edward Tiong said, the platform can analyze them against existing policies and contracts “in hours,” identifying gaps and action items for teams.

The company’s work with healthcare organizations covers more than 25 million covered individuals across 46 states, according to its website. Tiong said revenue has grown 10x. Read the full story here.

Oct. 14—Probably GeneticAI platform powering the research, diagnosis and treatment of genetic diseasesSeries: AAmount: $12 millionInvestors: Round led by Threshold, with participation from Y Combinator and other existing investors.

The company’s primary product is a physician-ordered genetic test for undiagnosed rare disease patients, who typically face a seven-year diagnostic odyssey before getting answers. There are two pathways to testing: free testing, through pharma partnerships, and insurance-billed testing. The free programs address specific conditions, with a limited number of tests available at a time.

Patients can check their eligibility by completing a health and diagnostic assessment online. Probably Genetic’s AI platform converts self-reported symptoms, medical records and biological data into phenotypic data that it hopes can be used to train AI models for precision medicine in the future. Thus far, it has collected data from 130,000 patients.

Probably Genetic said the fresh funds would be used to grow the core part of the business, for hiring and to enter the drug discovery arena. Read the full story here.

Oct. 14—AllaraVirtual women’s health providerSeries: UndisclosedAmount: $30 millionInvestors: Led by Index Ventures and GV (Google Ventures), alongside new investors Camino Partners, Foreground and Family Fund.

Allara, founded in 2020, has expanded to serve a broader continuum of women’s health. The company aims to fill gaps in care for women often navigating an array of specialists. Each Allara patient is paired with a multidisciplinary team, including OB-GYNs, endocrinologists, registered dietitians and patient success leads.

Since its expansion nationwide last year, Allara has added urgent care visits for things like UTIs, bacterial vaginosis (BV) and STDs, and brought on more internal medicine providers to its interdisciplinary care team. It has also launched more supplements and medication delivery services.

The new funding will accelerate enterprise partnerships, expand Allara’s clinical infrastructure and support more AI features, executives said. Read the full story here.

Oct. 14—Confido HealthStartup building an agentic AI operating system Series: series A extensionAmount: $12.5 millionInvestors: Z47, formerly Matrix Partners India, led the extension round. Existing investors Together Fund and Blume Ventures also backed the series A extension.

Confido Health is expanding beyond AI voice agents to build out an agentic AI operating system that can execute administrative workflows across a medical practice.

The series A extension follows its $10 million series A round announced in September to continue scaling an AI platform for end-to-end healthcare operations.

Confido Health integrates with over 50 systems of record, including electronic health records, practice management systems, phone systems, billing systems and fax, without requiring any change to a practice's existing tech stack. Confido's AI agents can increase administrative staff's capacity to serve patients by automating routine tasks like appointment scheduling, insurance verification, billing and patient outreach, according to executives.

Confido Health executives assert that its agentic AI operations platform can actually execute administrative work across existing systems, helping practices increase capacity and control labor costs rather than simply giving staff another software tool.

Healthcare private equity veteran Justin Saks joined as an investor and board advisor. Read the full story here.

Oct. 13—SukiAmbient clinical intelligence Series: EAmount: $90 millionInvestors: Healthier Capital, Crosslink Capital and Hercules Capital. All existing institutional investors also backed the round, including Venrock, Flare Capital Partners, Hedosophia, Philips Ventures and Zoom Ventures.

Suki CEO and Founder Punit Soni told Fierce Healthcare the company is investing in three areas with the fresh capital: advancing its AI, expanding its commercial organization and scaling its partner ecosystem.

The company has raised more than $250 million to date, executives say. Patient encounters supported by its tools grew more than 190% year over year in 2026, with revenue doubling in 2025 and on track for similar growth this year.

Suki now works with over 250 healthcare organizations and more than 30 technology partners that embed its AI into their platforms, executives say. Read the full story here.

Oct. 8—OutroEvidence-informed medication tapering supportSeries: Pre-seed and seed Amount: $7 millionInvestors: Listen Ventures, Cake Ventures, Jason Calicanis’s LAUNCH, Actions Capital, Hannah Grey VC, SemperVirens, Brock Recovery Group, Pave Health Ventures, and more.

Outro aims to support safe deprescribing of medications, starting with antidepressants. The company combines specially-trained clinicians with evidence-informed tapering protocols, patient monitoring, psychosocial support and technology. Its program is available in 14 states.

"Deprescribing guidance has existed in countries like the U.K. for years," said Mark Horowitz, M.D., Ph.D., Outro's co-founder, psychiatry researcher and deprescribing expert, in an announcement. "Yet in America, where antidepressant use is widespread, tapering support is very hard to come by, so millions of patients are left without support when they are ready to come off."

The funding will support the growth of Outro’s deprescribing clinician network, further the application of AI to deprescribing-specific workflows, expand the company’s tapering model into additional drug classes and grow existing partnerships with leading universities and advocacy groups.

Earlier this year, the Department of Health & Human Services announced a plan to prevent the unnecessary initiation of psychiatric medications and support tapering and discontinuation for patients not experiencing clinical benefit. It recommended providers regularly review the risks and benefits of psychiatric medications and offer alternatives like therapy when clinically appropriate. The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services also released guidance for providers on the importance of deprescribing.

Oct. 8—HealthleapClinical AI platform to flag undiagnosed conditionsSeries: seed/series AAmount: $38 millionInvestors: Sequoia Capital, First Round Capital and Hummingbird Ventures
